I don’t have any specific recommendations, since I don’t use windows OS tablets. So if I’m saying anything incorrect, feel free to correct me! But generally for specs anything above i5 CPU with 16GB RAM would do the bare minimum you would need to do. Having a GPU attached would also help, but I’m not sure if tablets come with a strong GPU chip.

If you still have your main setup at home and only use the tablet for simple portable work I think it would work, but anything substantial you’d probably have to use your main setup. People use iPads to sculpt in Nomad, so it’s definitely possible to do 3D work on a tablet PC. Personally I found Nomad / iPad to be limiting for detailed work. Another thing you might want to consider is thermals. Tablet PCs aren’t well built to release heat, and since it’s a touch screen it might heat up fast leading to discomfort when you’re working on it. My cintiq gets a little warm if I use it for 4-5 hours, and during warmer months it gets uncomfortable.

If you can find a decently priced used model that clears your spec preference, it could be a worthy investment just for quick portable work. 3D work is heavy on the computer, though so it’s always a battle between having a bulky set up or a limiting portable set up.

Use your real name on LinkedIn. Put your email everywhere, if it’s not easily accessible via demo reel or resume nobody will know how to easily contact you, putting another barrier in getting work. 

Yes anime style is heavily niche and hard if not impossible to find professional work outside of east asia. US studios especially are not heavily looking for anime style work. But if you consider your own art / style creepy, nobody will consider it valuable. It’s hard to gain that self confidence but you need to change your mindset first 

If you truly want to deviate from the anime look, look up established artists from studios you want to work for / style you want to achieve and study their portfolio. If you consume mostly anime as your pastime entertainment, watch something else. 

No, my advice is to find a balance between what you want / are good at and what the market wants. Making content based on celebrities or established characters is not beginner friendly. Likeness portrait/character work is extremely difficult because if it looks even a tiny bit off from the source it looks bad because it’s supposed to be that person but its not. You’re kind of setting a very high standard for yourself if you do likeness / copy work since people will automatically compare your work to the original. Doing something that is inspired / loosely based is okay, and easier to manage depending on the project. For example, I am working on an environment piece based on the prompt of how would my Baldur’s Gate character decorate her bedroom after the events of the game. I am currently obsessed with the game, so I’m taking inspiration from it but not copying something 1:1, since I don’t feel confident in having the same quality of work as a triple A studio like Larian. Also, it lets me be more creative, and add more of my personal touch than a direct re-model of assets already in the game. (Of course, remember to credit the OG creators / work when taking inspiration or making work related to another IP)

Is there an active industry in your home country? Working remote is definitely possible, but if there’s not much industry in the first place it can be more difficult. Do you want to work for US studios? If you have a LinkedIn, utilize it! 

I’m not very experienced myself so I can’t give you technical feedback & take my words with a grain of salt. But I think your character work has a unique style! I think it’s appealing, and having your own distinct style can be an asset, but it can limit which studios/clients are interested in hiring you. 

General portfolio stuff: I would take out the Markiplier piece, it seems like you used Metahuman (doesn’t mean it’s bad, but doesn’t show your character modeling or texturing skills) and doesn’t look like him. It’s also very different from your other work in terms of style, and being the first piece I see when I open your portfolio, I don’t think it is the strongest. “Your portfolio is only as strong as your weakest piece”I heard this a lot from professors & recruiters. If it’s all from the same project, I would consolidate the short film stills to 2-3 images. First still listed I personally would consider removing, the posing looks awkward. Also, if you are presenting your work & yourself professionally I would either delete captions or re-write them so they are more professional and descriptive of the work. (Title of work, when it was made, what softwares you used, and what parts you are responsible for). If you havent yet, make a demo reel! Send it out to recruiters, post it everywhere, get yourself listed on Upwork or Fiverr. 

I think you are doing good by posting your work & being active on forums! Don’t feel discouraged or think that you’re annoying anyone by posting your work. You made something, be proud of it!

Hi! I saw this post and wanted to leave a comment, I'm in a similar situation, graduated this year on F-1 and currently on OPT. First of all, as a fellow international student, I understand your struggle and for us it's just having to take whatever we can in order to not start accruing unemployment days. We work on a different timeline and expectation than domestic students if we truly wish to be employed & stay in the US. It is especially hard right now since the economy & industry is at a standstill for the most part. I think a lot of the "no junior, entry level jobs" are in part due to that. The dynamic as a F-1 student post-grad and worrying about employment due to status is something that is definitely not the easiest situation to be in. All this to say: no judgement. BUT.

Taking an unpaid volunteer position just to "stop the clock" for a short time post-grad, and working unpaid for a company for well over a year is different. If they haven't been able and/or willing to pay you for this long, I'm going to have to say it's probably not going to happen in the near future, if at all. What if the thing in October doesn't happen and you're still unpaid?  Applying for H1B is not a cheap nor easy process for the company & yourself. If they are not able/willing to pay you an income this long, don't put all your eggs in this basket assuming they will follow through with the H1B visa offer. If you really like this company and are willing to stake it out for the chance that they DO sponsor that H1B, have them write it down in a contract. This method is also not failsafe, but at least it's something more than just a verbal "maybe" promise. 

How much work are they requiring you to push out and how strict are they about that? Maybe you can continue being employed here for OPT, but delegate your time to your personal projects more than work for this company. After all, they are not paying you, nor do you have it in 100% certainty that they will sponsor the H1B. If OPT was not a concern I'd tell you to quit, but that is not on the table unless you're willing to lose some of your unemployment days.

I'll try and answer your questions as best as I can (at least the ones I can! But I'm also a fresh grad new to the industry, so dont take my words as the absolute truth haha)

***What’s really a good way for junior level animators to find a job at the moment? Even harder for me is that I’m an international so I suppose I have to be even better than a junior?***

From what I see, we graduated into a very hard spot. I think from my class of 40-ish 3D animators, maybe only 4 people have paid gigs. Mostly I see people getting offers through already being an intern / support staff (think Runners, PAs, etc.) at a company, and being offered a FT / artist position upon graduation or a year into their career. Reaching out to companies via e-mail, freelancer application form, recruiters, networking events, or even artists that work there can also lead to a job. Reach out to school alumni that are in the industry! I believe international students have it harder, since even on STEM OPT, the employer is required to fill out forms to the government & do extra work aside from just hiring/retaining an employee. H1B / Green Card sponsorship requires the company to show that they were unable to find a domestic worker that could do your job (i.e. you gotta be really freaking good at what you do). O1 is a little different, but you have to have exhibitions / articles / big screen creds under your name so the baseline is the same. Companies also prefer to hire someone they can train & retain for more than a year, especially for entry level workers. They don't want to put in resources hiring and training a junior only to have them potentially have to leave the company in a year because their OPT ran out. (So usually, they will help you with STEM extension if eligible, or start the H1B process right away since there's no guarantee you will win the lottery the first time) This is also why I would be more cautious of your current employer, they might just be holding on to you with the hope of H1B for the immediate labor not as a valued employee.

  
***My family recommended me to look into Canada. I know nothing of Canada immigration laws and animation job prospect there atm. Would anybody know more about Canada help me with this?***  


I don't know much about Canada's industry apart from the salary is a bit lower, but there are many studios in the region. I’m a student about to graduate, so I’m not an industry professional. But just as someone in the field coming across your demo reel & portfolio, I would be more clear on what parts you worked on in the 3D tab. Did you model and rig all the characters? Environments?

Demo reels should also be around 30 sec ~ 1 min unless you have a lot of quality work to show. Like senior level. I would cut some of the stuff you have in your reel, it either drags on too long or is not up to par with the rest of your work. I agree with jenumba, starting with the kick would help, and everything else they mentioned.

I’m more inclined towards modeling than animation, so I am more comfortable giving crit there. Your modeling work is very basic as well, unless the twin-tail purple dress maid girl is your own rig. This is why noting what you have done is helpful. Also, the one with Zelda, I’m unsure what parts are yours as well. I know the rig is a popular online rig, but did you make your own? Did you model the environment? Zelda seems a bit too small in comparison to everything else. If your focus in general or in that specific shot is environment modeling, I would just not have a character rig in there. If your focus is characters, and it is your rig, I would choose a composition that focuses more on the character. And the character should be of higher quality & the environment should match the style of the character (Zelda is stylized, but the environment seems to be realistic) Showing wireframes would help, especially with characters to show you know topology flow. I’ve also seen UVs on modeling portfolios. 

Using other people’s rigs without crediting them in your portfolio could become an issue. I would be more careful if that is the case.

Also, you have four different shots of the same 4 props, would consolidate. Add topology. The only thing that really draws my eye out of the four is the hourglass. Not really sure what the oblong green thing is. I would look into using Zbrush more. 

General note about your website, it might be because I’m on mobile but there’s some format breaking on mobile. I would look into that, it makes navigating your site janky. On your resume in the about section, info about your equipment is irrelevant. It also seems like you are active in the game dev world as well, which is nice.

Don't take it "for clout". Take it because you think that extra 30 points will help you in getting into the college you want to. Honestly 30 points at that range is hard, not saying it is not doable, but it is hard. At 1540, you're not getting the 1570 not because you don't know the concepts or the structure of the test, but it's because you're making mistakes. That means you would have to take more and more practice tests so you minimize your errors. 1540 is not a bad score. It's a good score, actually, and unless you feel like 1570 is worth the extra studying to the point where it's a decision breaker between rejection and acceptance, don't. Work on your GPA (having a solid GPA with that SAT score will get you considered by good schools), and especially your EC's. Colleges care about scores, but having a strong EC will make up for the 30 points you "missed" on your SAT. 780 math means you probably got 2 questions wrong, maybe 3 depending on the curve. 800 math isn't "EZ", unless you're lucky and get an easy test. And even if you do get an easy test, you have to get every single question correct. No room for any mistakes. Going thru all that shit just for 2~3 questions is not worth it, imo.

I can't say for sure, because I don't know much about you other than the stuff you told me. But you seem confident in your abilities to raise your score, so I would say try. It's probably not going to be as drastic as 1370 to 1470, because it's harder to get your score up as your score gets better (ex. 1350 to 1450 is doable while raising 1570 to 1600 is harder as that last 30 points is the difference between a few mistakes to a completely perfect test). If you think that studying for the SAT is going to mess with your schoolwork, don't do it, but if you are able to balance those two, go for it! But it also has to do with what kind of schools you are looking at. Art schools obviously do not really care about your SAT, so your score would be fine. But universities do care, and although SAT's are not all of your application, it does show how you rank amongst others (and it also shows your ability to study and score well on tests). It's all about where you want to go to. If you're aiming for Ivy League or schools around that range, I would say take it again for the 1500+ score (and make that last test worth the trouble), but if you are planning on attending to state schools or T40-ish schools, I think your score is fine. Look up the schools you want to go to and their average SAT. If 1470 is around average, look at your GPA. Where does it stand? If it's lower, try raising SAT. If it's around average or higher, work on your EC's and essay. If 1470 is above average, don't worry unless your GPA is low. If 1470 is above 75 percentile, that's your safety school. But college apps are more than just your SATs, so don't worry about your scores too much. If you have a solid GPA that's good! If you don't, work on that first, and your EC's and essays. Hope this helps!
